assumptions.statement: Households will keep a fridge and pantry inventory up to date inside an app on an ongoing basis.
assumptions.rationale: In the target segment of busy working families and working couples, keeping an inventory up to date is the riskiest operational barrier. In 1 of 4 in-target households (P02, sample size: 4 in-target households) and 2 adjacent households (P05, P10), participants explicitly stated they will quit immediately if logging requires manual cataloguing: 'Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two.' (P02:t8, P05:t8) and 'I think the biggest thing is not making it feel like homework.' (P03:t10, in-target family). If households do not keep inventory updated, the core engine cannot produce accurate plans or shopping lists.

assumptions.statement: Target households want an upfront structured weekly dinner plan rather than spontaneous same-day dinner suggestions.
assumptions.rationale: Weekly dinner planning fits weekly bulk grocery shoppers (3 of 4 in-target households: P01, P03, P04; sample size: 4 in-target households) who buy once a week. However, adjacent flexible couples (sample size: 2 adjacent households) actively reject rigid advance schedules: 'Planning ahead stresses me out. A plan I don't follow feels like failure, so I decide on the day.' (P05:t1) and 'I tried a meal-planning app once. By Thursday I hadn't followed the plan and I just stopped opening it.' (P05:t4). If the weekly-plan format induces guilt or rigidity, adoption will collapse outside strict bulk-shopping families.

assumptions.statement: The primary household pain point to solve is dinner arguments rather than shopping uncoordination and duplicate purchasing.
assumptions.rationale: The idea brief claims the app helps households 'stop arguing about "what's for dinner"' (idea_brief). However, arguing was reported by only 1 of 2 in-target couples ('Last Tuesday we got home at eight, argued for ten minutes about what to eat and ended up ordering pizza even though we had vegetables at home.', P02:t3; sample size: 2 in-target couples). In contrast, shopping uncoordination and buying duplicate ingredients was reported across 2 of 4 in-target households (P02:t4, P04:t4; sample size: 4 in-target households) and 1 adjacent flatmate household (P10:t2). Pitching relationship conflict resolution instead of shared shopping alignment targets a weakly supported need.

assumptions.statement: All multi-person households who cook at home on weeknights experience planning friction and food waste.
assumptions.rationale: The idea brief assumes any household of two or more people cooking weeknights is a prospective customer (idea_brief). However, evidence from 1 of 4 in-target households (P09, retired couple, sample size: 4 in-target households) shows established routines can entirely eliminate planning friction: 'We cook every day, we've done it for forty years. I know what we like and what is in the cupboard. Our daughter says we should use an app for the shopping list, but we have never needed one.' (P09:t1). Demographic qualification alone does not equal problem validation.

assumptions.statement: Households are willing to pay a recurring subscription between EUR 3.50 and EUR 6.99 per month for a meal-planning and inventory-tracking app.
assumptions.rationale: Median stated willingness to pay across cooking apps is EUR 3.50 per month (S05), and existing competitors charge from EUR 2.99 to EUR 6.99 per month (C:PlanPlate, C:MealLoop). In interviews, stated willingness to pay among in-target households (sample size: 4 in-target households) was conditional: P01 and P04 would pay 'a few euros a month' only if it demonstrably cuts grocery bills (P01:t9, P04:t9), P02 caps price at EUR 5-6 ('Maybe five or six euros. More than that and I'd just keep my notes app.', P02:t9), P03 prefers free with ads (P03:t9), and P09 refuses to pay anything ('Honestly I wouldn't pay for it. I'd want a free version.', P09:t9). App adoption is currently only 11% (S03).

assumptions.statement: Low-effort inventory capture technology (such as photo recognition or receipt scanning) can reliably parse multi-item fridge and pantry contents without frustrating manual corrections.
assumptions.rationale: FridgeChef uses photo recognition (C:FridgeChef) and PantryGenie uses barcodes (C:PantryGenie), but participants demand that setup not feel like homework (P03:t10) and reject typing in pantries (P02:t8). If optical or barcode capture fails to recognize perishable produce accurately or requires constant manual editing, the user burden will trigger immediate abandonment.

experiments.hypothesis: Households will sustain an active inventory for at least 14 days if initial setup and logging takes under 2 minutes using low-effort input methods rather than manual typing.
experiments.method: Recruit 20 in-target households (12 busy working families with children, 8 working couples who shop weekly). Provide a lightweight prototype or concierge tool testing three input methods: (a) snapping a photo of the fridge/produce drawer, (b) scanning supermarket grocery receipts, and (c) forwarding online grocery delivery orders. Track daily logging completion, time spent per update, and drop-off rates across 14 consecutive days without introducing a meal planner.
experiments.success_metric: At least 60% of participating households (12 of 20) maintain their inventory active through day 14 with an average input time under 2 minutes per session.

experiments.hypothesis: Weekly shoppers achieve higher plan adherence and lower meal-decision stress with a weekend-generated weekly plan, whereas flexible/daily shoppers achieve higher engagement with daily 'cook tonight from what you have' prompts.
experiments.method: Run a 2-week split test with 30 multi-person households (15 weekly shoppers and 15 daily/spontaneous shoppers). Group A receives an upfront weekly dinner calendar and consolidated shopping list on Sunday. Group B receives daily 4:00 PM prompts suggesting 2-3 fast recipes based strictly on on-hand perishables. Measure weekly recipe completion rate, reported decision fatigue, and abandonment rate in each cohort.
experiments.success_metric: Weekly shoppers achieve greater than 70% plan completion on weekly calendars; spontaneous shoppers show 50% higher active engagement and lower abandonment on daily suggestions compared to rigid weekly plans.

experiments.hypothesis: Messaging focused on avoiding duplicate grocery purchases and reducing wasted food drives higher conversion to a paid pre-order than messaging focused on ending dinner arguments.
experiments.method: Deploy a multi-variant landing page smoke test targeting multi-person cooking households. Test Variant 1 ('Stop arguing about dinner'), Variant 2 ('End duplicate grocery buys and coordinate shopping'), and Variant 3 ('Turn your fridge into dinner and stop throwing away food'). Each page includes subscription pricing tiers at EUR 3.99/month and EUR 4.99/month with a 'Start 14-day trial' pre-order call to action.
experiments.success_metric: Variant 2 or 3 achieves at least a 5% click-to-preorder conversion rate at EUR 3.99/month, significantly outperforming Variant 1.

open_questions: Which input modality (refrigerator shelf photo, barcode scan, supermarket receipt scan, or online grocery order integration) provides the lowest user friction and highest accuracy for inventory onboarding and maintenance?
Does any user segment sustain digital meal planning beyond week one, or does retention drop sharply across all cohorts?
Whether an upfront weekly meal calendar or a same-day 'what can I cook tonight' recommendation model generates higher long-term user retention.
Who within the multi-person household acts as the primary decision-maker for dinner planning versus who executes grocery purchasing and pays for digital subscriptions?
What are the actual churn rates, active user bases, and customer satisfaction levels of existing competitors like MealLoop, SupperSync, and FridgeChef?
What is the total addressable market size, geographic variation, and household income profile for the target segment of busy weeknight home cooks?
Can optical ingredient recognition accurately parse loose produce and opened containers without requiring manual text corrections from users?
recommendation_reason: PantryPal should test further before building the planner. While household food waste is verified (households discard 19% of purchased food, S01; weekly groceries average EUR 118, S02) and adults spend 22 minutes daily deciding meals (S04), the core foundational assumptions remain unvalidated. Crucially, keeping a manual inventory updated is the riskiest usability barrier: users explicitly reject cataloguing pantries as homework (P02:t8, P03:t10). Furthermore, the weekly planning format alienates flexible households who experience rigid plans as stress and failure (P05:t1, P05:t4), and stated willingness to pay is fragile and capped below EUR 6.00/month (P02:t9, S05). Building the complete planner now risks developing an unmaintainable product. The team must first test low-effort inventory input mechanisms and compare weekly versus daily planning formats through lightweight prototypes.
